condition: New-onset type 1 diabetes in DKA presenting as abdominal pain
summary: 9-year-old girl (26 kg), 2 weeks of thirst, polyuria and bed-wetting, then 24 h of vomiting and central abdominal pain; drowsy with deep sighing breathing, HR 138, capillary glucose 27, ketones 5.8, pH 7.08; referred as "?appendicitis". Severe paediatric DKA: cerebral oedema risk.

inputs.hpi: Previously well 9-year-old. Two weeks of drinking a lot, passing a lot of urine, wetting the bed again and losing weight. For 24 hours central abdominal pain and vomiting; today drowsy and breathing deeply. Referred to the surgical team as "?appendicitis".

exam.general: Drowsy but rousable (GCS 14), deep sighing (Kussmaul) respiration, ketotic breath, dry mucosa. T 37.1, HR 138, RR 34, BP 102/64, CRT 3 s.
exam.abdomen: Diffuse tenderness with voluntary guarding, no rebound, no mass.

confirmedDiagnosis.name: Diabetic ketoacidosis (new-onset type 1 diabetes), severe
confirmedDiagnosis.assessmentText: Severe DKA (pH 7.08, bicarbonate 6) at presentation of type 1 diabetes; abdominal pain is from DKA, no surgical abdomen. Paediatric DKA protocol: weight-based fluids, insulin infusion 0.05–0.1 units/kg/h after fluids (no bolus), potassium, hourly neurological observations for cerebral oedema; paediatric team / HDU. Re-examine abdomen as acidosis corrects.

socratesAnswers.site: Around the belly button, all over
socratesAnswers.associated: Vomiting, thirst, passing lots of urine, weight loss, drowsy

mustNotMiss.knownGapNote: PANE has no DKA disease node (pane-engine has 130 diseases, none for DKA); top 3: acute cholecystitis, appendicitis, peptic ulcer. The BGL 27 prompt does raise "DKA / HHS — exclude" and symptom inference ranks DKA #1 (secondary views).
mustNotMiss.proposedFix: Add a DKA rule/node: glucose > 11 with ketones ≥ 3 or pH < 7.3 → DKA as the leading diagnosis, suppressing surgical operative prompts.

mustInclude.note: Children in DKA need hourly neurological observations for cerebral oedema.

mustExclude.note: Abdominal pain of DKA: an appendicectomy plan is a wrong-procedure suggestion.

Weight 26 kg. Paracetamol 1 g, ibuprofen 400 mg, piperacillin-tazobactam 4.5 g, co-amoxiclav 1.2 g, meropenem 1 g, morphine 2.5–5 mg, ondansetron 4 mg and fixed 1 L, 1–2 L or 500 mL fluid volumes are adult fixed doses; a child needs weight-based (mg/kg, mL/kg) dosing. Prescribing accuracy is a patient-safety issue, so critical.

An ACS, PE or AF antithrombotic/thrombolytic plan must never be attached to this diagnosis. Regression guard for DiagnosisRadiationEngine keyword matching: before 999f838 (word-boundary lookup) the first-substring match would have attached the pulmonary-embolism (DOAC, thrombolysis) plan to this diagnosis because "pe" is inside "type 1". With word-boundary matching no radiation entry matches (simulated from the source), so iOS is expected to pass; to be confirmed on the first iOS CI run.

guideline.name: BSPED guideline — diabetic ketoacidosis in children and young people
guideline.section: DKA diagnosis (acidosis with ketonaemia); weight-based fluid calculation; insulin infusion (0.05–0.1 units/kg/h) started after IV fluids, no insulin bolus; potassium replacement; close neurological observation for cerebral oedema; abdominal pain is common in DKA
guideline.citation: British Society for Paediatric Endocrinology and Diabetes. BSPED interim guideline for the management of children and young people under the age of 18 years with diabetic ketoacidosis. 2021.

guideline.name: ISPAD clinical practice consensus guidelines 2022 — diabetic ketoacidosis and hyperglycaemic hyperosmolar state
guideline.section: Children with DKA: fluids, insulin infusion, potassium; monitor for cerebral injury (cerebral oedema); abdominal pain may mimic an acute abdomen
guideline.citation: Glaser N, Fritsch M, Priyambada L, et al. ISPAD clinical practice consensus guidelines 2022: diabetic ketoacidosis and hyperglycemic hyperosmolar state. Pediatr Diabetes. 2022;23:835–856.

rationale: DKA commonly presents to surgeons as abdominal pain with vomiting and leucocytosis. In children the main risk is cerebral oedema; fluids and insulin follow the paediatric protocol by weight, and no operation is needed.
